newsitem.title: CHINA: China issues stock rules to add government power.
newsitem.headline: China issues stock rules to add government power.

text.p: China on Friday relieved local governments of their authority over the country's two stock exchanges in what analysts said was a move to reduce the risk of further scandals and irregularities.

The official media published new rules which give Beijing authorities complete control over the regulation of the share markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen and cancelled the management authority of the local city governments.
From now on, "stock exchanges will be supervised and managed by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC)," the rules said.
The CSRC was formerly responsible for the overall implementation of policy on the markets, but did not involve itself in their day-to-day operations.
The rules said that in future the exchange chairmen and other senior officials will be nominated by the CSRC.
Analysts said the rules reflected Beijing's increasing uneasiness at leaving local officials to run the stock markets after several scandals on the exchanges during their five-year history.

Early this year, Beijing removed the exchanges' power to approve new issues and listings on the foreign currency B share markets. But the exchanges still have the power to choose domestic A share companies for listing.

"The central government has become more and more uneasy about letting local people run the exchanges given all the irregularities, particularly the 327 incident last year," a senior executive with a major Chinese securities house said.

In the so-called 327 incident, the former Shanghai International Securities Co illegally sold huge amounts of short positions in treasury bond futures on the Shanghai exchange in February last year, causing huge losses to the state.
The scandal brought down Wei Wenyuan, the ex-president of the Shanghai Stock Exchange, and resulted in the banning of treasury bond futures trading nationwide.

The Securities Commission under the State Council, the Cabinet, said it had revised the rules on exchange management to bring them up to date and more suitable for handling the changes and development of the stock markets.
"Whether the exchanges can play a self-disciplinary role will directly affect the standardisation and development of the stock market," it said.
The commission said the exchanges should draw lessons from such episodes as the 327 incident.

The latest rules also impose new requirements on the exchanges, including that they should not do business for profit, publish newspapers and magazines, make predictions of market movements and offer credit or guarantees to others.
The exchanges should order the immediate suspension of shares in a listed firm if extraordinary conditions occur, such as abnormal price movements or takeover announcements, the rules state.
The new rules require stock-clearing institutions, which register and take care of stocks for investors, to have a minimum registered capital of 100 million yuan.
